newsitem.title: FRANCE: BoF nominees may lead to faster cuts - economists.
newsitem.headline: BoF nominees may lead to faster cuts - economists.

text.p: The appointment of two new members to the Bank of France's monetary policy council may lead to slightly faster interest rate cuts but the Bank's commitment to the stability of the franc and European monetary union will remain solid, economists said on Friday

The government said earlier Pierre Guillen and Jean-Rene Bernard would replace Jean Boissonnat and Bruno de Maulde, whose mandates on the council expire next week. Prime Minister Alain Juppe said the appointments did not imply any change in policy.

Economists said while Guillen and Bernard are both allies of president Jacques Chirac and would probably favour lower rates, they were chosen more because the government wanted to create a balanced council rather than signal any major policy change.
"These nominations reinforce diversity on the monetary policy council," Herve Goulletquer at Banques Populaires, said.

"Either opposition to (Bank of France governor Jean-Claude) Trichet is being created which could lead to more openness to lower rates... (or) another reading is that we're getting people with a different view, who may think differently," he said.
"It could be rather a good thing that we don't have a whole council of people who think alike," he said.

Some said the appointment of the two Chirac allies was a warning shot at Trichet, who sparred with the French president during his election campaign, letting him know he wouldn't always be allowed to have his own way.
"It's a signal to Trichet - putting in people who won't follow him blindly, even if there is no change in monetary policy," Jean-Louis Mourier of Louis Dreyfus Finance said.

Eric Chaney, economist at Morgan Stanley in Paris, said while the broad lines of French exchange rate policy would remain unchanged the shift in the balance of the council now opened the door to French rates moving below German rates.
"The Bank of France is likely to cut rates faster than before, at least until the German repo (rate) level is reached," he said.
"Whether the Bank of France could try to cut rates below the German level is now an open question whereas before it was not."

The intervention rate, which sets the floor for French money market rates, is at 3.15 percent, just above the key German repo rate at three percent, and most economists have said Trichet would be reluctant to allow rates to pass below German rates.

However two of the current members of the Bank of France monetary policy council, Jean-Pierre Gerard and Paul Marchelli have both said there was scope for a further French rate cut without a German move. And one banker said this was now likely.

Jean-Michel Naulot, a banker close to National Assembly President Philippe Seguin, told Reuters, "The nominations which have just been made at the Bank of France clearly signify one thing, that a decision has been made to bring French short-term rates below German rates in the coming months."

Chaney said such a move would be negative for both the franc and long-dated bonds and could send 10-year yields on French bonds, currently seven basis points below 10-year Bund yields, above their German counterparts.
"I think there's a 40 percent chance, and in my view it would be negative for French markets, it would weaken the currency and the bond market," Chaney said.
